title: The Transporter
full_review:
Mindless mayhem is the name of the game in the ludicrous action flick, "The Transporter" (20th Century Fox).

Directed by Corey Yuen as if absurd plot contrivances were desirable, the movie is little more than a series of violent confrontations between the title character (Jason Statham as a shady courier) and up to a dozen thugs at a time, who of course are all demolished by Statham's macho moves with his flying fists and lacerating limbs. When he's not battling hand to hand, one-on-one (or one-against-12), there are plenty of rat-a-tat-tat shootouts and explosive bombs to wake those tired from all that fierce fighting.

Providing bland window dressing is Shu Qi as a kidnap victim the transporter reluctantly rescues. Despite his not wanting to save her, she insists on thanking him with her sexual favors. She's also preoccupied hating her evil father (Ric Young, looking like he's already been embalmed -- and he'll need to be once his daughter catches up with him). She wants to foil her father's plot to smuggle immigrant slave labor into the south of France. Somehow the transporter gets enmeshed in all of this, becoming a target of the father and his many -- but not mighty -- minions.

The choreography of the fight scenes is impressive and Francois Berleand brings a smidgen of dry Gallic wit to the proceedings as a French police detective willing to overlook the transporter's criminal activities in order to crack the smuggling ring.

However all the convenient coincidences, ridiculously extended chase scenes and utterly bogus emotions add up to a film that is in no way transporting.

Because of excessive violence, an implied sexual encounter and a few instances of profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
